title: Redwood Optimize walkthrough - batching & KV cache (Triton Payments)

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-05-05
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~49 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Triton Head of ML), Laura Gomez (Platform), Jin Park (CTO), Maya Ortiz (Security)

Summary: Quick Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and KV/prefix cache. Ran through cost model scenarios, recommended pilot configuration and asked for prompt distribution + benchmarks.

00:00 Alex Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we've got about 45 minutes — gonna run through Redwood Optimize, batching and prefix/KV cache recs, and leave time for q's
00:12 Samir Patel: thanks, Alex; quick context — we're a payments infra, peak 600 rps but most is low-latency ops, typical gen requests ~120 tokens, maybe 10% are >1k tokens, so cost is starting to spike
00:28 Priya Nair: ok great, that distribution's exactly what matters for batching and KV cache savings — if 90% are short with common prefixes we can get big wins
00:42 Laura Gomez: our infra is k8s on AWS; we currently run internal Triton endpoints for some models and are evaluating switching to Redwood for production because of cost predictability and observability
00:55 Jordan Lee: quick note, Triton to us is the customer name not the Triton runtime? (laugh) — got it.
01:05 Alex Chen: yeah haha, small collision. So, two levers: batching (reduce GPU idle time / higher throughput) and prefix/KV cache (skip recomputing prefixes for similar conversations). We'll walk numbers from a simple cost model
01:22 Samir Patel: what are realistic latency tradeoffs for batching — we can't tolerate >200ms p95 for auth flows
01:32 Priya Nair: good question — small dynamic batches (size 4-16) with latency SLOs can still keep p95 under 200ms for short prompts; for auth we'd prioritize low-latency routing (dedicated low-latency pool) and use caching aggressively for repeated prompts
01:50 Laura Gomez: what about our long tail 10% of large prompts, do they kill batching efficiency?
01:58 Jordan Lee: they do reduce average batching efficiency; we often route long sequences to a separate pool (higher memory GPUs) and shorter ones to a high-throughput pool. Redwood supports policy routing, so you can split by seq length or route by API key
02:15 Samir Patel: walk me through prefix cache vs KV cache — we use a lot of templated prompts with customer-specific tokens at the end
02:24 Priya Nair: prefix cache typically saves the KV cache state for the model after a shared prefix; it's great when you have many prompts that share the first N tokens. KV cache is similar term here: store the attention key/value tensors so you don't recompute. Redwood's Optimize suggests seeding a KV cache with top prefixes (we often do top 5-10k prefixes) and it can reduce token compute by 40-70% depending on overlap
02:45 Samir Patel: 40-70% is a big range — what assumptions give you 70%?
02:52 Priya Nair: that's when 60%+ of your requests fully reuse a cached prefix of ~50-100 tokens; also depends on how you quantize and batch
03:10 Alex Chen: quick numbers example: assume 10M requests/day, avg request 120 tokens, 1 GPU hour cost... (high level). If we cache the first 60 tokens for 50% of traffic, you save those tokens compute — we modeled a 45% reduction in total token compute in our spreadsheet sample. We'll send the calc after this call
03:34 Laura Gomez: can you share the spreadsheet now?
03:37 Alex Chen: we'll send it after the call — action item.
03:45 Jin Park: curious about memory overhead for keeping 10k prefixes online — does that require a lot of memory or network storage?
03:53 Jordan Lee: each cached KV entry is model-dependent but for a 1k-token prefix it's several MBs; 10k prefixes could be tens of GBs, so we recommend starting with top 2-5k and monitoring hit rate. You can also offload cold prefixes to a backing store and have an LRU in memory
04:15 Maya Ortiz: on security, how are these caches encrypted and who has access? We need KMS + audit logs for any private deployments
04:24 Priya Nair: Redwood supports KMS integration (customer-managed keys) and audit logs for cache operations in Private/Dedicated. For hosted we have envelope encryption and SOC2 controls. We'll share SOC2 and the architecture notes; that's in the next steps
04:40 Samir Patel: what's the recommended quantization level — do you support 8-bit and does that change cache behavior?
04:48 Jordan Lee: 8-bit or 4-bit quantization reduces memory and compute, improves throughput. Cache stores are still based on model KV tensors; with quantized kernels we store quantized tensors (smaller). There's a small accuracy tradeoff to test — we'll recommend model-level evals during pilot
05:05 Alex Chen: demo time — Priya, can you show the Optimize console view we referenced?
05:12 Priya Nair: sure — (describes UI) here we have token breakdown per route, a batch simulator where you can plug in qps and seq distribution and it simulates costs, and a cache-hit heatmap. In this run we show 50k qps? sorry 50 rps sample, showing a 48% token compute reduction with top-3k prefixes seeded
05:38 Samir Patel: the simulator numbers are helpful — how accurate are they vs real runs?
05:44 Priya Nair: we calibrate against baseline runs on similar workloads; expect 10-15% variance depending on prompt churn and exact runtime kernels
06:00 Laura Gomez: can you expose cache hit metrics in our own monitoring? We want to feed hits into Prometheus
06:06 Jordan Lee: yes, Redwood emits per-route cache-hit, cache-miss, and batch-latency metrics; we have integrations for Datadog/Prometheus and can push to your cloudwatch as well
06:18 Samir Patel: for the pilot, what would Redwood recommend for the dedicated pool sizing? We have ~600 peak rps with 120 tokens average and burst 2x
06:26 Priya Nair: rough rule: for short tokens on A100-style instance, one GPU can handle ~300-600 qps depending on batch config and quantization. For your numbers I'd propose starting with 2 GPUs dedicated for low-latency routes (auth) plus an autoscaling high-throughput pool for the rest. The cost model in the spreadsheet has a sample calc. Start small and scale during pilot
06:48 Jin Park: are there auto-scaling knobs and cost caps?
06:52 Alex Chen: yes, Dedicated has autoscaling policies and burst capacity, and you can set max GPUs and a cost alerting threshold in the console
07:05 Maya Ortiz: what's the SLA for dedicated vs hosted?
07:10 Alex Chen: Dedicated has SLA-backed latency and uptime; hosted has standard availability but fewer guarantees. We'll include specifics in the doc we send
07:20 Samir Patel: a technical Q — with KV cache, how do you handle cache invalidation when model updates or revs happen?
07:28 Jordan Lee: good point — we version caches per model version. When you rollout a new model, you can warm caches by replaying top prefixes or run an on-demand re-encoding job. We also support TTLs and manual invalidation APIs
07:45 Laura Gomez: is it easy to A/B different quantization profiles and measure quality regressions? We need a way to guard output quality
07:52 Priya Nair: yes, Optimize ties to evals; you can run prompt subsets and measure semantic similarity / quality regression alerts. We can gate rollout with canary percentages and automatic fallback on quality drop
08:10 Samir Patel: what about multi-region routing for disaster recovery?
08:16 Alex Chen: Redwood supports geography routing and fallback; caches are regional but can be pre-warmed across regions if you want cross-region redundancy (costs more)
08:30 Jin Park: Ok, let's talk numbers — can you run through an illustrative cost model on the call?
08:35 Priya Nair: sure. Baseline: 10M requests/mo * 120 tokens = 1.2B tokens. If compute cost per token on the model is X, but with a 45% token compute reduction from caching + batching we get effective compute of 660M tokens. If GPU-hour pricing plus utilization leads to $Y baseline, this reduces to $Y * 0.55. In our spreadsheet example for a mid-sized model that equates to ~45% reduction in spend. The spreadsheet shows per-route breakdown, and we also include the small added infra cost for 10k prefix cache memory (eg +$Z/month)
09:10 Samir Patel: are we talking per-token cost or per-GPU-hour? We need conversion to our current internal cost basis
09:17 Alex Chen: we'll map to GPU-hour and to your current Triton cost assumptions in the spreadsheet. We'll need your average GPU instance pricing or we can use public benchmarks
09:26 Laura Gomez: do you have any customers in payments space with similar patterns?
09:31 Alex Chen: yes — we anonymized Aurora and Mariner Payments examples in the sheet; they saw 30-60% savings depending on cache hit rates and routing splits
09:45 Samir Patel: ok can Redwood run a short pilot using our sample workload?
09:51 Alex Chen: yes — recommended pilot: 2-week run, route 20-30% of traffic to Redwood Dedicated pool, seed KV cache with top prefixes, run parallel telemetry. We'll do baseline -> optimize run comparisons
10:05 Jin Park: what's the onboarding time and what access do you need?
10:09 Priya Nair: minimal: sample prompt CSV, API keys if you do hosted, or access to VPC peering info for Private/Dedicated. We'll provide a pilot runbook; typically 1-2 weeks to get meaningful numbers depending on your infra team's availability
10:27 Maya Ortiz: for security review, what about SSO/SAML and tenant isolation for auditability?
10:33 Alex Chen: we have SAML/SSO for Console, RBAC, per-customer audit logs and dedicated VPC options for Private deployments. We'll send the security pack
10:45 Samir Patel: if we see 50% compute reduction is there any vendor lock-in risk from seeding KV caches?
10:54 Jordan Lee: cache logic is application-level; if you migrate, you can export prefix lists and keys. Cache entries are not proprietary — the effort is mostly re-seeding and running a short warmup
11:12 Priya Nair: some practical tips: start with top 1-2k prefixes, measure hit rate and marginal savings per 1k prefixes added; tune TTLs to balance miss rate vs memory cost; use dynamic batching with latency caps for auth paths; quantize non-critical routes aggressively
11:35 Samir Patel: what about observability — can we break down cost by customer/merchant (multi-tenant)?
11:41 Alex Chen: yes per-route costs can be broken down and attributed to API keys or tenant ids; console has that built-in and you can export raw usage tables
12:05 Laura Gomez: ok last bit — what's the expected exit criteria for pilot success?
12:12 Alex Chen: agree on cost reduction target (e.g., 30% net compute cost) + no regression in p95 latency for auth flows; also security sign-off and infra connectivity verified
12:30 Jin Park: timeline — if we start onboarding next week, we could have pilot numbers in ~2 weeks
12:36 Alex Chen: great; we'll send the spreadsheet and SOC2 docs today. Priya will run the baseline sim and Jordan will help with any infra questions
12:50 Samir Patel: thanks everyone, this was useful

(occasional crosstalk and filler, some ASR errors: "Reedwood" instead of Redwood at 29:11 in the full audio, names sometimes garbled.)

Recap:
- Pilot: seed KV cache with top prefixes, 2-week pilot routing 20-30% traffic, start with 2 GPUs for low-latency routes
- Primary goals: 30-50% compute reduction target, maintain p95 latency <200ms for auth flows, security/compliance review
- Next: Alex to send spreadsheet, Priya to run sims, Samir to share prompt distribution and seq stats

End of transcript.
